records.summary: Atsuomi entered electoral politics after a failed first campaign and advanced through Naoe patronage and ethically compromising assignments.
Naoe is the party secretary-general and a dominant internal power broker who can subordinate senior colleagues and influence factional relations.
At the project launch period the Citizens Party has major factions associated with Naoe, Isomaru and Prime Minister Miyako, and an emerging fourth faction under Kijima.
Kijima has a prominent public reformist image and growing popularity among younger party members; Naoe identifies him as a greater political threat than Isomaru.
Atsuomi describes high political achievement as shaping stakeholder satisfaction despite unmet demands, not merely delivering what voters initially ask for.
Naoe assigns Atsuomi a secret human-resource-development project; Kamogawa is attached to assist, despite Atsuomi reservations.
A stated political goal of the project is to cultivate future cadres linked to wealthy families and loyal to the Naoe faction.
records.caveat: Plan rather than an established outcome.

records.summary: Naoe refuses direct financing and even the public use of his name, leaving Atsuomi to construct financing and operating arrangements while maintaining secrecy.
Naoe directs Atsuomi toward Sakayanagi as a potential bridge to the financial world; Sakayanagi family ties intersect with the Kijima sphere.
Sakayanagi is alert to the danger that information he receives could be carried to Kijima, while Atsuomi deliberately accepts an uncertain allegiance risk.
Tsukishiro presents himself as an independent general-purpose operative handling protection, intelligence and other sensitive work, not merely Naoe bodyguard.
Tsukishiro later studies Atsuomi background and negotiates a relationship based on his expectation that Atsuomi will survive political conflicts.
Sakayanagi agrees to introduce funding contacts in exchange for the right to observe the White Room operating methods.
Sakayanagi voices humanitarian objections to educational methods that erase or suppress emotion and refuses to regard academic results as sufficient.
Naoe decides to abandon his leadership bid and support Kijima, then demands that Atsuomi suspend the White Room project and withdraw from political prominence.
Atsuomi outwardly accepts Naoe order to terminate the project while privately resolving to preserve his power and eventually overcome his former patron.
Tsukishiro interprets Naoe conduct as fear of Atsuomi growing too powerful and says Naoe intended Atsuomi to remain subordinate to Naoe political heir.
records.caveat: Tsukishiro explanation is not independent omniscient confirmation.

records.summary: As Naoe influence removes supporters, Atsuomi sustains the White Room through a smaller pool of financiers and organized solicitation events.
The White Room fundraising event gathers wealthy families and company heirs; their children display status conflicts and existing family networks.
Atsuomi later retains financial influence even outside elected office, while maintaining a political return plan as Naoe health deteriorates.
At the end of the volume Atsuomi commissions future arrangements from Tsukishiro, while the details are not fully disclosed in the scene.
records.caveat: Do not invent exact undisclosed details of the plan.

records.summary: Atsuomi considers deploying Kiyotaka in politics but acknowledges both the nepotism interpretation and Kiyotaka difficulties with ordinary emotional interaction.
Atsuomi keeps his options open regarding opposition-party contacts but resists becoming a mere tool for rival politicians.
The Naoe faction uses hierarchical discipline, intimidation, deliberate waiting and patronage as signals of rank.
The project begins as a secret early-development institution meant to educate children from infancy and present that achievement as politically and financially valuable.
An abandoned pharmaceutical factory in an isolated part of Saitama becomes the selected facility after renovation.
Atsuomi names the institution White Room partly for the clean, pure visual symbolism of the uniformly white interiors.
The financing model solicits wealthy benefactors and parents of children they wish to conceal or educate; investors often expect status or future influence.
Mika helps Atsuomi obtain compromising private information about prominent men through contacts in nightlife venues.
records.caveat: Do not assume all people discussed were in the same faction.

records.summary: The recruitment pipeline includes children relinquished by parents, clandestine arrangements through the Ooba network and contact points presented as help to distressed mothers.
The recruitment approach seeks very young infants, including some older than the strict newborn definition, and plans extensive medical monitoring before education.
Parents who surrender children are expected to have severely restricted contact; adult reunions or departures are treated as exceptions or later milestones.
The first experimental intake includes fifteen infants randomly assigned in groups of five to Ishida, Suzukake and Souya; Tabuchi supervises comparative evaluation.
The first cohort deliberately compares three distinct educator strategies in isolated groups, with a lead instructor selected from results.
Suzukake group initially obtains superior academic and attention-test results, and Atsuomi selects Suzukake as educational leader for later generations.
Suzukake uses punitive educational methods, including physical mistreatment, while Sakayanagi objects and Atsuomi prioritizes results.
Suzukake curriculum specifies ten escalating difficulty levels, with later cohorts initially given progressively harder level assignments.
For the fourth generation Atsuomi rejects the planned level-four path and instead imposes the more demanding Beta curriculum despite researchers warning about survival.
The ordinary level-four curriculum moves to the fifth generation, while the special Beta protocol remains attached to the fourth generation.
Research reports partial early-cohort attrition and improvements relative to earlier cohorts, but these are time-specific measurements rather than universal education laws.
The fourth generation starts with seventy-four children, decreases to approximately fifty around age five, later to Kiyotaka and Shiro, then finally Kiyotaka alone.
records.caveat: Age and exact count should not be applied to other cohorts.

records.summary: White Room days are meticulously timed from morning wake-up through instruction, physical training, medical checks and nighttime sleep with monitoring equipment.
Curriculum includes language, mathematics, political science, economics and physical exercise; other passages add instruments, traditional arts and combat sports.
A VR-like travel curriculum seeks to simulate outside environments but causes Kiyotaka physical discomfort; not every exercise is experienced as useful by him.
After a travel-class disruption, a card-based exercise probes attention, pattern identification, observation and memory through task design.

The fourth-generation training includes judo, randori and physical exchanges against adult instructors; later adult sparring includes a scene where weapons (baton, stun gun or knife) are offered under instructor authority and Kiyotaka chooses the baton. Do not attribute the offered weapons to the adults or presume improvised weapons.
The facility includes a heated pool for training; instruction, performance targets and optional free-time swimming are distinguished within sessions.
Children are subjected to selection cutoffs, elimination after insufficient results, and punishments independent of the daily academic requirements.
Researchers consider competition against Kiyotaka difficult to calibrate and discuss restricting disclosure of his performance to other cohorts.
Sakayanagi visits the facility and sees a restricted presentation, while Atsuomi orders staff to avoid exposing visitors to the harshest training.
As cohorts advance, Suzukake adopts communication components from the fifth generation onward despite acknowledging tradeoffs in measurable progression.
The account reports a fifth-level curriculum for generation six, sixth level for generation seven with total reported dropout, and mixtures of fourth and fifth for later cohorts.
Suzukake regards Kiyotaka as an exception and says the project has not demonstrated an ability to reproduce his unique development on demand.
Suzukake describes unresolved nature-versus-nurture questions and acknowledges severe deficiencies in Kiyotaka emotional and everyday social competencies.
The White Room temporarily halts activities amid political pressure; Kiyotaka is moved out while Atsuomi plans future arrangements.
Upon suspension, Suzukake records a research video dated March 11; the narrative date should not be converted into a real-world civil year.
Atsuomi explicitly considers financially backed children separately from other graduates for whom independent transition arrangements are expected.
records.caveat: Character dialogue and planning does not prove every case was implemented.

records.summary: Atsuomi acknowledges White Room students can provide political agents or loyal personnel for his future influence, beyond the institution public educational justification.
Parents and financiers can request exceptional meetings with children; Yuki parent arranges a later clinic reunion with Kiyotaka as part of her treatment context.
Atsuomi learns that patronage, affiliation and backroom assignments are essential to his advancement despite nominal electoral ideals.
Atsuomi manages Kamogawa impatience, teaches political etiquette and warns against visible breaches of protocol.
Atsuomi remains alert to surveillance and resists tempting intelligence collection that he assesses would be exposed.
Kamogawa follows instructions and contributes to identifying and arranging an isolated facility while seeking Naoe approval.
Sakayanagi conditions cooperation on observing the institution rather than simply accepting Atsuomi account of it.
Tsukishiro elicits Atsuomi background, assesses his persistence and offers sophisticated operational services.
Suzukake challenges alternative researchers and advances a punishing performance-driven education system.
Sakayanagi rejects claims that results alone justify conditioning away emotional development.
Atsuomi exploits staged images of apparent paternal devotion as financial-promotion material when Kiyotaka is brought to the facility.
Kiyotaka at age two detects task-design ambiguity in a candy-location exercise, evaluates hypotheses and reacts to being wrong as a learning problem.
Kiyotaka can perform written academic assessments rapidly and accurately but sometimes strategically withholds performance to examine other children.
Kiyotaka explains the desire to observe those who struggle as an opportunity to understand differences, while instructors initially interpret it as compassion.
records.caveat: His stated explanation is not objective proof of complete absence of concern.

records.summary: Yuki initiates unsolicited conversation about food and later demonstrates emotional expression that fascinates Kiyotaka.
Kiyotaka reaches to prevent Yuki falling; the event precedes his investigation of spontaneous smiles.
Kiyotaka uses environmental cues to infer a concealed mechanism in a card exercise, eventually obtaining a perfect observed result.
Kiyotaka acknowledges some children learn new physical tasks faster initially, but believes his structured practice closes the difference.
Yuki is judged below the current fourth-generation cutoff and desperately asks to remain; Kiyotaka challenges the consequences and is punished.
Shiro privately says he will voluntarily leave the White Room to pursue freedom, friends and experiences the institution cannot provide.
Kiyotaka does not stop Shiro from departing and thereafter becomes the only remaining fourth-generation student.
In combat against adult opponents Kiyotaka considers differences in strength, reach and weapon selection rather than assuming superior raw strength.
Kiyotaka explains severe combat outcomes through the literal orders he believes he received; institutional personnel react with alarm.
Arisu, as a child visitor, questions whether extreme White Room performers reflect an innate genetic advantage rather than the facility itself.
An Amasawa-company president uses the White Room as an arrangement for children born outside his marriage and expresses limited desire for contact.
Kanzaki Ryuuji initially avoids intervening in a dispute over a claimed autograph, perceiving the alleged liar behavior as relevant and confrontation as undesirable.
Ishigami Kyou disputes an accusation by separating photographic evidence of a meeting from proof of who did or did not receive an autograph.
Ishigami prompts his would-be attacker to grasp his collar before loudly calling for help, making the aggressors visible to adults.
Ishigami explains why he did not ask Atsuomi for help: Atsuomi had observed the bullying without acting, so the boy doubted he would intervene.
Ishigami father expresses interest in placing his son near Atsuomi future political work rather than requiring him to inherit the company.
Atsuomi challenges Kanzaki Ryuuji to consider strategic benefits of helping even when he lacks a personal stake in a conflict.
After a long separation Yuki shows lingering distress linked to White Room experiences and seeks comfort from Kiyotaka, who does not provide the response she hopes for.
Kiyotaka initially performs compliance with Atsuomi directions while internally planning to preserve independent options.
Atsuomi stage-manages appearances and investor narratives, separating public philanthropy from political and personal objectives.
Atsuomi rejects treating dropout statistics as absolute educational triumph and evaluates the economic and political burden of failures.
Atsuomi refuses to permit sentimental involvement with his child to distract from public relations or operational goals.
Kamogawa shows emotional dependence on Atsuomi political fortunes and continues working with him after Naoe withdrawal.
Tsukishiro supplies strategic interpretation of the Naoe-Kijima transition and remains linked to Atsuomi later plans.
Suzukake views fourth-generation singular performance as potentially irreproducible and resists treating one exceptional child as proof of universal artificial-genius production.
Naoe appears to use delays, rank and political dependence to impose terms; Atsuomi sees himself both protected and trapped by the relationship.
Mika collects private intelligence in situations where political targets underestimate women working in nightlife.
Sakayanagi maintains cordial contact with Atsuomi even after their philosophies diverge, and provides access to other social and financial networks.
Tsukishiro tells Atsuomi that Kijima political strategy also includes education-related ambitions; this is Tsukishiro account, not a specification of an ANHS policy.
Atsuomi and his associates consider shifting patronage systems and the risk that sponsorship networks can follow the dominant power broker rather than declared loyalties.
Company President Kanzaki expresses interest in financing the project despite earlier inability to gain a prominent role in its initial funding.
Atsuomi at one stage regards Naoe political seniority and family succession plan as obstacles to his own pursuit of national leadership.
Mika and Atsuomi agree to have their biological child raised through the White Room; financial terms and guardianship documents are part of their arrangement.
Mika names the baby Kiyotaka when Atsuomi asks her for a name before final registration arrangements.
Atsuomi describes the arrangement with Mika in transactional terms, including a substantial cash payment and an expected end to their marriage.
The White Room recruits specialists with professional expertise but reputational and interpersonal problems, rather than prioritizing conventional public-facing teaching profiles.
Tsukishiro is described as simultaneously supervising project risk on behalf of Naoe and assisting Atsuomi, creating an explicit dual-role conflict.
Atsuomi privately suspects Tsukishiro involvement in a journalist disappearance, but the exact actions are not established through independent first-person confirmation.
records.caveat: Never promote suspected homicide attribution to a verified event.

records.summary: An Amasawa-company sponsor discusses placing another child into the White Room while one daughter is already cared for there; this does not by itself identify either child by name.
records.caveat: Do not auto-link to Ichika without explicit identifying evidence.

records.summary: Sakayanagi and Arisu are given observation access, with the visit exposing competing moral and scientific interpretations of the White Room experiment.
White Room operators track heart rate and other physiological measurements during challenging tasks, but observations must not be reinterpreted as complete access to internal emotions.
Dropout is an institutional category covering loss of eligibility to continue White Room curriculum; some former students later live outside and have ongoing psychological difficulties.
Atsuomi maintains surveillance or deliberately limits information disclosed to external observers such as Sakayanagi to protect the project from political or reputational threats.
White Room observed apparent educational performance differences between research groups and cohorts, but sample size, survivor bias and shifting tasks limit causal interpretation.
Mika chooses Kiyotaka name and signs a prearranged guardianship and financial separation agreement, while Atsuomi treats the arrangement instrumentally.
Tsukishiro accurately anticipates Atsuomi call and shows detailed knowledge of his situation, creating a power imbalance before their meeting.
Tsukishiro refuses to be intimidated by Atsuomi anger and frames clandestine actions in terms of protecting political principals.
Souya arrives at a hiring interview wearing a lab coat and speaks candidly about having been rejected by his earlier institution.
Tabuchi carries comparative-evaluation responsibility but shows nervousness about organizational fundraising; Atsuomi reframes risk to stabilize him.
At an observation visit Arisu explicitly questions whether a child innate talent rather than institutional training explains an exceptional result.
Sakayanagi sees concern for Kiyotaka emotional growth and social circumstances as a reason to critique the institution despite admiration for its ambitions.
Arisu mother is referenced as an important positive comparison for Arisu intellectual and personal qualities, without giving a comprehensive profile of her in the passage.
Ishigami at the sponsors event distinguishes evidentiary uncertainty from immediate safety, responding to imminent physical threat via the adult audience.
Kiyotaka at the later meeting with Yuki rejects the idea that an obligation exists merely because adults request his presence and makes an independent decision to leave.
A girl named Mikuru struggles during harsh judo training, is struck by an instructor and loses consciousness; this is a concrete observation of abusive conditions.
The young politician Kisarazu is mentioned as obtaining an expensive apartment financed by advantageous connections; this is an anecdote told by Kamogawa.
Mika contacts Sophia to obtain information about Sonezaki, a wealthy married man, for potential coercive leverage.
Atsuomi asks Mika to approach Sasada as his position rises; Mika resists because of Sasada prior unwelcome conduct toward her.
Nogi threatens another child by invoking his father corporate power, and the intimidation collapses when adults respond to a visible physical confrontation.
The children dispute an autograph allegedly issued by a public figure named Kazuya; neither the allegation nor its negation is conclusively established merely by a photo of another meeting.
records.caveat: Treat as contested child testimony, not verified signer behavior.

records.summary: The clandestine Ooba group has links to infant procurement, and Atsuomi considers its members capable of serving whichever political side protects them.
